clinicalPearls: A minority of Meniere disease is familial, defined by more than one affected member within a family and often earlier onset
The core phenotype is recurrent spontaneous vertigo with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, aural fullness, and tinnitus
Familial cases may show anticipation-like earlier onset in successive generations and a higher rate of bilateral involvement
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, and several candidate genes have been implicated
Comorbid migraine and autoimmune conditions cluster in affected families, supporting a multifactorial basis
Diagnosis remains clinical, with genetics used mainly to inform counselling rather than to make the diagnosis
Management mirrors sporadic disease with lifestyle and dietary measures, vestibular rehabilitation, and stepwise medical or procedural options
reference.pathophysiology: Meniere disease is characterised pathologically by endolymphatic hydrops, an excess of endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth, thought to reflect impaired endolymph regulation and periodic disturbance of inner-ear fluid homeostasis. In familial disease an inherited predisposition, most often transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance, lowers the threshold for this dysregulation, and clustering with migraine and autoimmune disease suggests shared susceptibility pathways. Fluctuating distortion of the cochlear and vestibular sensory epithelia produces the episodic vertigo and the characteristic fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, which may become fixed and bilateral as the disease progresses.
additionalDifferentials: Enlarged vestibular aqueduct with fluctuating loss
additionalInvestigations: Serial pure-tone audiometry to document fluctuating low-frequency loss
Detailed family history and pedigree for affected relatives
Vestibular testing including caloric and video head impulse assessment
Cross-sectional imaging to exclude retrocochlear pathology
Delayed-contrast inner-ear imaging for hydrops where available
Screening for comorbid migraine and autoimmune disease
redFlags: Asymmetric or unilateral progressive loss raising concern for vestibular schwannoma
Bilateral progression toward disabling hearing and balance loss
Sudden profound hearing loss requiring urgent assessment
Neurological features suggesting a central cause of vertigo
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and episodic, often with eventual stabilisation of vertigo but a tendency to progressive and sometimes bilateral hearing loss, so familial cases warrant longer-term audiovestibular monitoring.
pitfalls: Overlooking vestibular migraine, which frequently coexists and mimics the disorder
Failing to reassess for asymmetric loss that could indicate a schwannoma
Assuming a clear genetic test will confirm or exclude the clinical diagnosis
Neglecting counselling about bilateral risk in affected families
references: Barany Society Consensus: Diagnostic Criteria for Meniere's Disease
management: Reduce endolymphatic hydrops burden with dietary salt restriction and, where used, betahistine and a diuretic to lessen attack frequency
Relieve acute vertigo attacks with vestibular sedatives and antiemetics such as antihistamines or a short benzodiazepine course
Escalate refractory unilateral disease with intratympanic corticosteroid, and intratympanic gentamicin chemical ablation for disabling vertigo when hearing preservation allows
Consider surgical options such as endolymphatic sac decompression, labyrinthectomy or vestibular neurectomy for intractable vertigo
Rehabilitate hearing loss with hearing aids and offer vestibular rehabilitation for chronic imbalance
Identify and treat comorbid migraine, which clusters in affected families
Maintain longitudinal audiovestibular monitoring with serial audiometry and provide genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance
